title: Beef
question: Is grass-fed beef worth it?
decision: 100% grass-fed or grass-finished, no added hormones, with a certifier’s seal.
why: The whole-food standard is grass after weaning, no grain, and no feedlot.
short_answer: On a beef label, ‘grass-fed’ alone rests on the producer. FSIS reads ‘100% grass-fed’ as grass after weaning, no grain, and pasture access. A certifier’s seal is what audits it. That one is worth paying for.
detail: The USDA withdrew its own grass-fed marketing standard, the AMS Grass (Forage) Fed claim standard, in 2016, so the bare claim now rests on the producer and on whatever third-party seal sits behind it. American Grassfed Association certification and Certified Grassfed by AGW both audit the whole life. The compositional difference that follows a grass finish is established and modest, and it is a leaner animal with a different fatty-acid balance rather than a different food. The fat profile follows the finish, not the start.

title: Rotisserie chicken from the hot case
aliases: what is in a rotisserie chicken
is the deli rotisserie chicken injected
question: Is the rotisserie chicken worth buying?
decision: Chicken and salt on the label: buy. Phosphate and starch: pass.
why: Every ingredient must be listed in descending order; a solution names its percent and contents.
short_answer: A rotisserie bird is a plain chicken or a solution bird. A plain one is chicken with salt and spices, roasted in the store. A solution bird was pumped with a seasoning solution before the spit. The sticker says which.
detail: Two label rules do the work. 9 CFR 381.117(h): a raw poultry product with added solution must carry a descriptive designation stating the percentage of added solution as a number with the % sign, e.g. ‘contains 15% added solution of water and salt’, plus the common or usual name of every solution ingredient in descending order; the word ‘enhanced’ may not appear in the product name. 9 CFR 381.118(a): any poultry product fabricated from two or more ingredients lists them by common or usual name in descending order of predominance; ingredients at 2 percent or less may trail the list under a ‘contains 2% or less of’ line. 9 CFR 424.21 permits sodium and potassium phosphates in poultry ‘to decrease the amount of cooked out juices’, capped at 0.5 percent of total product, and sodium hydroxide only alongside phosphate at one part to four. FSIS’s labeling glossary defines a bone-in bird injected or marinated with broth, water, fat or flavor enhancers as ‘basted’ or ‘self basted’, about 3 percent solution, with the solution ingredients named on the label. At the shelf the two kinds read differently: a plain bird’s panel is one line (one store’s organic rotisserie chicken lists ‘organic chicken’ and nothing else); a solution bird lists water and its seasoning after the chicken, in descending order as 381.118 requires; a phosphate, a starch and a sweetener are the usual entries. On the sticker, the second word on the list settles it: ‘salt’ or ‘spices’ is a plain bird; ‘water’ followed by ‘sodium phosphate’, ‘modified food starch’, ‘sugar’ is a solution bird, roasted. Both are cooked chicken. One of them is also a marinade injection.

title: Ground beef
question: What ground beef lean ratio should I get?
decision: Organ blend with each organ’s percentage first, then ground beef with nothing added.
why: Federal rules keep added water, binders, and organs out of ‘ground beef’, so a blend carries its own name.
short_answer: Pick an organ blend that prints each organ’s percentage, or ground beef with nothing added. How the cattle were raised is on the Beef card.
detail: Both ‘ground beef’ and ‘hamburger’ cap at 30% fat, so the name is where the difference lives. ‘Ground chuck’, ‘round’ or ‘sirloin’ names the cut it came from. The ingredient list should be beef, with seasoning at most. ‘Ground beef’ may not contain added water, phosphates, binders or extenders, and may not have beef fat added as such. ‘Hamburger’ may. The ratio on the pack is lean to fat by weight. 80/20 is 20% fat; 90/10 is leaner. The name ‘ground beef’ allows no added water, phosphates, binders or extenders. 9 CFR 319.15(a) defines ‘Ground Beef’ as chopped fresh or frozen beef, fat capped at 30 percent, no added water, binders or extenders, with trimmed cheek meat the one allowed addition and capped at 25 percent. A product with liver or heart in it falls outside that definition, and 9 CFR 317.2 then requires a common or usual name or a truthful descriptive designation plus a full ingredient statement in descending order. ‘Ancestral blend’ and ‘primal blend’ are producer names for exactly this product, not standardized terms. Two label examples: one blend states 8 percent organ meats (4 percent liver, 4 percent heart, 92 percent muscle); another states 92 percent ground beef, 5 percent liver, 3 percent heart. Liver is the retinol-dense ingredient: the NIH fact sheet lists pan-fried beef liver at 6,582 mcg RAE per 3 ounces, against a tolerable upper intake of 3,000 mcg a day for adults. The liver percentage on the label is therefore the number that matters. A blend that states its shares is plain ground beef with a measured amount of organ folded in. A blend that hides behind ‘organ blend’ or ‘ancestral’ alone leaves the liver share unknown. A blend carries its own descriptive name and a full ingredient list. By NIH figures, 3 ounces of pan-fried beef liver holds more than twice the adult daily vitamin A upper intake. Producers print shares such as 8 percent organ, or 5 percent liver plus 3 percent heart. Organs are part of eating the whole animal, and a blend puts them in a familiar grind.

title: Eggs
aliases: Pasture-raised organic corn- and soy-free eggs
question: What do cage-free, free-range, and pasture-raised eggs actually mean?
decision: Pasture-raised, organic, and corn- and soy-free, all three together.
why: Hens eat what they are given; the carton words show that feed and that life.
short_answer: Look for pasture-raised, organic, and corn- and soy-free together. Next is soy-free organic pasture-raised, then organic pasture-raised. A certifier’s seal backs the pasture claim.
detail: Both ‘soy-free’ and ‘corn-free’ have to be printed outright, because nothing else on the carton implies them, and most cartons never do. The claim clusters on small regional brands, farm stands and farmers markets rather than on the national pasture-raised labels, so the supermarket case is often the wrong place to look for it. Organic reaches the ration from a different direction: organic feed, no GMOs, no routine antibiotics, no added hormones. Pasture-raised paired with a third-party certification (Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved) is a real and audited claim about space, the strongest of the space words, and it still sits below feed here. Cage-free and free-range are weaker again, and the words on their own are not worth paying up for. Cage-free, free-range and pasture-raised describe how much room the hen had and whether she got outside, and not one of them says a word about what went in the trough. The standard is all three on one carton: what she ate, how it was grown, and how much room she had.

title: Produce
question: Is organic produce worth the extra money?
decision: Organic for produce eaten whole; conventional for produce you peel.
why: Residue sits on the surface, so whatever gets thrown away takes it along.
short_answer: Organic earns the money where the skin gets eaten: berries, leafy greens, apples, grapes, potatoes. Anything peeled goes in conventional, even the ones that feel delicate: avocado, kiwi, mango, banana, citrus, onion.

title: Freezing what is about to turn
question: How do I freeze produce before it goes off?
decision: Enzymes keep working in the freezer until heat switches them off.
why: Enzymes keep working below freezing and turn color and flavor. A brief scald ends them.
short_answer: Freezing slows a vegetable down. It does not switch it off. The enzymes behind ripening and browning keep working in the freezer, slowly. Sixty seconds in boiling water switches them off.
detail: Unblanched, a bag of beans comes out gray and tasting of hay months later, because the enzymes kept working. After the scald, the job is keeping air and ice crystals away from the food. Fruit is the exception and it is a real one: the enzymes that matter in fruit mostly affect appearance rather than flavor, and blanching would cook the texture out, so berries, banana and stone fruit go in raw. For vegetables the sequence is scald, chill hard in ice water to stop the cooking, dry, then freeze in a single layer before bagging. A tray first keeps the pieces separate instead of fusing into one brick you have to break with a knife. Air is the other enemy: what is called freezer burn is water subliming off the surface and leaving it dried and oxidised, and pressing the air out of the bag is most of the defense. Very high-water vegetables collapse whatever you do.

title: Getting residue off conventional produce
question: Does washing actually get the pesticide residue off?
decision: Baking soda in the water lifts residue a plain rinse leaves.
why: A rinse moves dirt. Bicarbonate breaks residue down, and it needs minutes to do it.
short_answer: Baking soda breaks down some pesticide residues on the skin. Running water mostly moves them around. It takes twelve to fifteen minutes in the bowl, not thirty seconds under the tap. Residue already in the flesh stays.
detail: A soak does what a rinse cannot. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and it degrades some residues on the skin, where running water mostly relocates them. It is a surface treatment and only a surface treatment. The study everyone is quoting applied two pesticides to organic Gala apples and compared tap water, a one percent baking soda solution, and the bleach solution used commercially. The same work is where the limit comes from: thiabendazole was mapped eighty micrometers into the fruit and phosmet twenty, and nothing applied to the outside reaches that. A later comparison across apples, grapes, lemons and strawberries put baking soda alone lower and found a commercial product ahead of it, so the honest position is that the soak beats water and the ranking against bottled washes is not settled.

title: Reviving wilted greens
question: Can I bring limp greens back, or are they finished?
decision: Limp greens have lost water, not gone bad, and they come back.
why: The cells have gone slack. Given cold water they refill and the leaf goes rigid again.

title: Gluten-free bread
question: How do you pick gluten-free bread?
decision: Gluten-free bread carrying the label claim, with its flours and binder read.
why: Four label wordings share one federal gluten limit. The claim covers gluten only, so the flours and binder still matter.
short_answer: “Gluten-free”, “no gluten”, “free of gluten” and “without gluten” all meet one federal limit. The claim is voluntary. Bakers replace gluten with blended flours and starches, plus a gum that binds the loaf.
detail: Under 21 CFR 101.91, all four wordings mean the food has less than 20 ppm (parts per million) gluten. Wheat starch may appear only if the food stays under 20 ppm. The claim is voluntary, defined by an FDA rule issued in 2013. Bakers replace gluten with a blend of flours and starches, such as rice, potato or tapioca. A hydrocolloid binder, usually xanthan gum or HPMC, mimics some of the stretch gluten gives. “Gluten-free” describes gluten content only.

title: The bread aisle
question: What bread should I buy?
decision: Pick the bread type first, then read the first flour for “whole”.
why: The first ingredient and the Whole Grain Stamp tell a whole grain loaf from a refined one.
short_answer: Pick the type first: sandwich, sourdough, sprouted, gluten-free or buns. Then read the first ingredient for “whole”. “100% whole wheat” or “100% whole grain” on the label can be trusted.
detail: The Whole Grain Stamp comes in three tiers. The 100% Stamp means all the grain is whole, with at least 16 g per serving. The 50%+ and Basic Stamps mean at least 8 g per serving.
